about.title: Egypt II: Hieroglyphs, Religion and Law
about.length_note: This runs a little over 40 minutes. It covers six topics, and each one is taught as say it, explain it, give an example, then check it. Every step has a pause for a question. It splits cleanly into two sittings: stop after the Rosetta Stone beats (writing) and start again at 'Gods and temples'.

say.text: Welcome to class five. Last time we met the Nile and the pharaoh. Today: how Egypt wrote, worshipped, buried its dead and kept order.

show.text: Egypt II: Hieroglyphs, Religion and Law

say.text: Six steps today, one at a time. Writing. The Rosetta Stone. Gods and temples. Burial. Pyramids and tombs. Then law.

show.text: 1. Writing | 2. The Rosetta Stone | 3. Gods, temples, priests | 4. Burial and the afterlife | 5. Pyramids and tombs | 6. Law and ma'at

say.text: Start with hieroglyphs. They are Egypt's picture writing. Some signs stand for an idea. Other signs stand for a sound.

show.text: Hieroglyphs

say.text: They developed around 3200 BCE. In time they became the script of monuments and temples.

show.text: about 3200 BCE

ask.q: A hieroglyph sign could stand for what?
ask.right: Either an idea or a sound
wrong: Only a sound, like a letter in English
Only a decoration with no meaning
ask.why: Hieroglyphic signs were sometimes ideograms (ideas) and sometimes phonetic (sounds).

say.text: Here is an example. A king's name was written inside an oval ring called a cartouche. The signs inside spell the name by sound.

show.text: An oval ring around a row of small picture signs: a royal name written in a cartouche.

say.text: Carving signs takes time. So scribes made a faster form, called hieratic. It is a simplified, joined-up version of the same signs.

show.text: Hieratic

say.text: Scribes wrote hieratic with a reed brush and black ink, on papyrus. Scribes were the trained writers in palaces and temples.

show.text: A scribe sitting with a reed brush and a papyrus sheet, writing quick, flowing signs.

say.text: Example: a scribe might use hieratic for a ledger or a contract. If the same text went on a tomb wall, he would switch to formal hieroglyphs.

show.text: Ledger or contract on papyrus: hieratic | Tomb wall or temple wall: hieroglyphs

ask.q: A scribe is writing a grain ledger on papyrus. Which script is he most likely to use?
wrong: A picture painted on a tomb wall
None, because Egyptians kept no records
ask.why: Hieratic was the quick everyday script for ledgers, contracts and letters. Formal hieroglyphs were kept mostly for monuments and tombs.

say.text: A third script came later. Around 700 BCE, an even quicker script called demotic took over from hieratic. Hieroglyphs stayed in use for sacred and monumental writing.

show.text: 3200 BCE hieroglyphs | soon after: hieratic | about 700 BCE: demotic

say.text: Later still, Egyptian was written with Greek letters. That form is called Coptic. It spelled the end of hieroglyphs in daily use.

show.text: Coptic: Egyptian in Greek letters

say.text: One important point. Hieroglyphs are a script, not a language. There was one Egyptian language, written in several scripts.

show.text: One language | Hieroglyphic | Hieratic | Demotic | Coptic

ask.q: How many ancient Egyptian languages were there in these scripts?
ask.right: One language, written in several scripts
wrong: Four languages, one for each script
Hieratic was a language and hieroglyphs were not
ask.why: The Egyptian language was written in hieroglyphic, hieratic, demotic and Coptic scripts. A script is the writing, not the language.

say.text: Now a real example of everyday writing. Merer was a middle-ranking official, and he kept a logbook on papyrus about 4,500 years ago.

show.text: A papyrus logbook: rows of small hand-written signs recording daily boat trips.

say.text: His log records crews shipping limestone from the Tura quarries to the Great Pyramid. It dates to about the 26th year of King Khufu.

show.text: Merer's crew | limestone from Tura | to Khufu's pyramid

say.text: Archaeologists found these papyri in 2013, in caves at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea coast. They are the oldest papyri found in Egypt.

show.text: About 4,500 years ago: Merer writes his log | 2013: papyri found at Wadi al-Jarf

ask.right: Hauling limestone to the Great Pyramid
ask.why: Merer's log records his crew moving limestone from Tura to Khufu's pyramid.

say.text: How did we learn to read hieroglyphs again? The key was one famous stone.

show.text: The Rosetta Stone

say.text: The stone carries one decree in three scripts: hieroglyphic, demotic and ancient Greek. It was written in 196 BCE, under King Ptolemy V.

show.text: A dark stone slab with three bands of writing, one above another.

say.text: French troops found it in 1799 at Rashid. The British took it after defeating France, in 1801. It has been in the British Museum since 1802.

show.text: 196 BCE: made | 1799: found by French troops | 1801: British take it | 1802: British Museum

ask.q: When was the Rosetta Stone made, and when was it found?
ask.why: The decree was written in 196 BCE. French troops found the stone in 1799, so the date made and the date found are about 2,000 years apart.

say.text: Here is the clue. Scholars could already read Greek. So they could compare the Greek with the Egyptian parts of the stone.

show.text: Greek: readable | Demotic: unknown | Hieroglyphic: unknown | Same decree in all three

ask.q: Why was the Greek text so helpful?
ask.right: Scholars could read it, giving a way into the other two scripts
wrong: Greek was the oldest script on the stone
Greek told them the names of the gods
The Greek text was a dictionary of hieroglyphs
ask.why: The same decree appears in three scripts. Because scholars could read Greek, they could use it to unlock the other two.

say.text: An English scientist, Thomas Young, made early progress. He published in 1819 and linked the signs in the cartouche to the sounds of Ptolemy's name.

show.text: Thomas Young: the first steps

say.text: The French scholar Champollion knew Coptic. He saw it as a late form of the Egyptian language. He combined that with Young's method.

show.text: Champollion and Coptic

say.text: He announced his decipherment on 27 September 1822. He recognised that the signs were sometimes ideas and sometimes sounds.

show.text: 27 September 1822

ask.q: What did Champollion learn about the hieroglyphic signs?
ask.right: Some stood for ideas and some for sounds
wrong: All of them were only pictures of objects
All of them were letters, like English
ask.why: Champollion saw that the writing mixed signs for ideas with signs for sounds.

say.text: So who gets the credit? Young made early progress. Champollion took it further and is widely credited with cracking the code.

show.text: Young: early steps, 1819 | Champollion: full breakthrough, 1822

say.text: Writing is done. Now religion. Egypt had many gods. A temple was a house for a god, and each temple had one main god.

show.text: Gods and temples

say.text: People believed the god lived in its statue, in a shrine deep inside the temple.

show.text: A small stone shrine in a dark inner room, holding a statue of a god.

say.text: That inner room was the darkest and most enclosed part, with the highest floor. It protected the statue and recalled the mound of creation.

show.text: Darkest room | Enclosed | Highest floor | Protects the statue | Recalls the mound of creation

ask.q: Where did Egyptians believe a god lived in its temple?
ask.right: In its statue, in the shrine
ask.why: Gods were believed to live within their statues in the temple's shrine.

say.text: Priests served the gods. A priest's duty was to care for the god of his temple. They did not preach or hold weekly services.

show.text: Priests: caring for the god

say.text: Many temples had a sacred lake, where priests bathed to be pure. Apart from the high priest, most priests were part-time.

show.text: Sacred lake: bathing to be pure | Most priests: part-time

ask.q: What was a priest's main duty?
ask.right: To care for the god of his temple
wrong: To preach weekly sermons to crowds
ask.why: Egyptian priests tended the god's needs. They did not preach or run weekly services for the public.

say.text: Ordinary people usually could not enter the inner parts. But at festivals, priests carried the god's statue out in a boat-shaped shrine called a barque.

show.text: Priests carrying a boat-shaped shrine through a crowd.

say.text: People could ask the god a question. If the barque rocked forward, the answer was yes. If it rocked backward, no.

show.text: Barque rocks forward: yes | Barque rocks backward: no

say.text: Caring for the gods was every pharaoh's duty. Temples were designed to reflect and maintain the universe. Keep that idea of order in mind; it returns.

show.text: Order of the universe

say.text: Now burial. Egyptians believed that after death came a new kind of life. They would need their bodies and their belongings.

show.text: The afterlife

say.text: So they preserved the body. This is called mummification: preparing the body so it does not decay.

show.text: Mummification

say.text: Embalmers removed the moist parts that rot, and dried the body. Then they wrapped it in linen over 15 days, while spells were said.

show.text: 1. Remove the parts that rot | 2. Dry the body | 3. Wrap in linen, 15 days, with spells

say.text: A full elite mummification took about 70 days. Ancient methods varied; there is no single surviving instruction manual.

show.text: Days in an elite mummification

ask.q: Roughly how long did a full elite mummification take?
ask.why: The whole process took about 70 days. The 15-day figure is only the wrapping stage.

say.text: The embalmers left the heart in the body. Egyptians saw the heart, not the brain, as the centre of wisdom, feeling and memory.

show.text: The heart stays

say.text: They believed the heart could reveal your true character, even after death. That is why it was kept.

show.text: The heart was left in the body so it could be weighed in the afterlife.

ask.q: Which organ was left in the body, and why?
ask.right: The heart, because it was thought to be the centre of thought and character
wrong: The brain, because it held memory
The liver, because it was the lightest organ
ask.why: Egyptians believed the heart, not the brain, was the source of wisdom and memory. It had to stay for the judgement.

say.text: The coffin went into the tomb with possessions and small model workers called shabtis. They were meant to work for the dead.

show.text: Possessions | Shabtis: model workers | A priest touches the coffin's face to restore speech, sight and hearing

say.text: Then came the judgement. The dead person's heart was weighed on a scale against the feather of Ma'at. Anubis watched over it.

show.text: A balance scale: a heart on one side, a single feather on the other, and a jackal-headed god beside it.

say.text: A heart that balanced the feather meant entry to the afterlife. A heavy heart was eaten by the monster Ammit.

show.text: Heart balances the feather: allowed in | Heart too heavy: eaten by Ammit

say.text: People even placed heart scarabs in the tomb. A spell on them begged the heart not to speak against its owner.

show.text: A carved scarab beetle placed with a mummy, inscribed with a spell.

ask.q: What was the heart weighed against?
ask.why: In the weighing of the heart, the dead person's heart was set against Ma'at's feather.

say.text: Now a key word: Ma'at. It means order, truth and what is right. Egyptians pictured it as a goddess.

show.text: Ma'at: order, truth, what is right

say.text: Living by ma'at was thought necessary to pass the Hall of Judgment into the afterlife.

show.text: Truth | Order | Balance | Justice

ask.q: Ma'at is best described as what?
ask.right: The ideal of truth, order and justice, personified as a goddess
ask.why: Ma'at personified order, truth and what is right. Her feather was used in the judgement of the dead.

say.text: Now pyramids. A pyramid was a king's tomb. The Great Pyramid is the tomb of Khufu. Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure built the three big ones at Giza.

show.text: Pyramids: royal tombs

say.text: Khufu ruled about 2589 to 2566 BCE. His pyramid's ancient name was Akhet-Khufu, meaning 'Horizon of Khufu'.

show.text: About 2589 to 2566 BCE: Khufu rules, Great Pyramid built

say.text: Why did the giant pyramids stop? Mark Lehner notes that the effort was enormous. There were only about five giant pyramids, and later ones got smaller.

show.text: about 5 giant pyramids

say.text: Who built them? Many people picture slaves. The Greek writer Herodotus, about 2,000 years later, wrote of gangs of 100,000 men forced to work in turns. Later retellings turned them into slaves.

show.text: Herodotus: gangs of 100,000 forced workers?

say.text: Archaeology points elsewhere. The builders were more likely skilled, well-compensated craftsmen plus manual labourers. All were well fed.

show.text: Workforce numbers given for the Great Pyramid

ask.q: What does the evidence say about who built the Giza pyramids?
ask.right: Egyptian workers, skilled craftsmen and labourers who were well fed
ask.why: Excavations show Egyptian workers who were fed and housed, and buried near the monuments they built.

say.text: How do we know? In 1991, Mark Lehner found two ancient bakeries near Giza. They led to a whole town.

show.text: 1991: the bakeries

say.text: The team dug a 4,500-year-old town where stoneworkers, weavers and bakers lived. Zahi Hawass dug the workers' cemetery.

show.text: About 4,500 years ago: workers' town lived in | 1990s: bakeries and town found, workers' cemetery dug

ask.q: What did the bakeries and the town tell archaeologists?
ask.right: The pyramid builders lived in an organised town and were fed
wrong: The pyramids were built by robots
ask.why: Bakeries, a town and a cemetery show an organised, well-fed workforce, not an army of starving slaves.

say.text: Later, kings stopped building giant pyramids. At the time of Tutankhamun, kings were buried in underground tombs in the Valley of the Kings, to protect them from thieves.

show.text: Old Kingdom: giant pyramids at Giza | Later: underground tombs, Valley of the Kings

say.text: Most of those tombs were looted in ancient times. Tutankhamun ruled about 1333 to 1324 BCE and was buried in a small tomb hastily converted for him.

show.text: A narrow stairway cut down into rock, leading to a small sealed doorway.

say.text: His tomb's location was forgotten, so it escaped most robbery. Howard Carter's team found it in November 1922.

show.text: About 1324 BCE: Tutankhamun buried in KV62 | November 1922: tomb found by Howard Carter's team

ask.q: Why was Tutankhamun's tomb found so intact?
ask.right: Its location was forgotten, so later robbers missed it
wrong: It was sealed inside a giant pyramid
No one had ever entered it at all
ask.why: Britannica notes his burial place was forgotten. The tomb was entered and briefly plundered, but it was mostly intact when found in 1922.

say.text: Last topic: law. Egyptians believed law was handed to people by the gods at creation. Ma'at, truth and order, was the ideal behind it.

show.text: Law and ma'at

say.text: No Egyptian law code survives. But legal documents like deeds and contracts do survive.

show.text: No law code, but legal documents

say.text: So how were cases decided? By the king's decrees, and by earlier cases used as precedent. English law works in a similar way today.

show.text: King's decrees | Earlier cases (precedent)

ask.q: Does a complete Egyptian law code survive?
ask.right: No, so historians use decrees, contracts and court records
wrong: Yes, carved on a stone at Giza
ask.why: No legal code survives from ancient Egypt, only legal manuscripts, inscriptions and letters that show how law worked.

say.text: At the top was the pharaoh, the final authority in disputes. Next was the vizier, who directed the government, sat in judgment and appointed magistrates.

show.text: Pharaoh: final authority | Vizier: judge and chief official | Magistrates and councils

say.text: The vizier was called a priest of ma'at. The pharaoh judged the worst crimes, sometimes after the vizier investigated.

show.text: Vizier: priest of ma'at

say.text: Local cases went to councils called kenbet. Officials who judged also did other jobs, and no special court building was set aside.

show.text: Kenbet: a council of officials

say.text: In court there were no lawyers. People spoke for themselves, showed documents, and sometimes called witnesses.

show.text: Speak for yourself | Show documents | Call witnesses

say.text: Men and women could both own and leave property, go to court, and bear witness.

show.text: Men and women could sue and own property

ask.q: In an Egyptian court, who spoke for you?
ask.why: Parties to a dispute were not represented by lawyers. They spoke for themselves and presented evidence.

say.text: Law even protected tombs. Records of tomb-robbery trials from the 20th Dynasty survive.

show.text: Tomb-robbery trials

say.text: The tomb of the vizier Rekhmire, from about 1400 BCE, holds a long text on a vizier's duties.

show.text: A painted tomb wall at Thebes covered in hieroglyphic text: the Installation of the Vizier.

say.text: Compare with Mesopotamia. There we have law codes such as Hammurabi's. Egypt has none, but its law ranks with Sumerian law as among the world's oldest surviving systems.

show.text: Mesopotamia: law codes such as Hammurabi's | Egypt: no code, but decrees, precedent and documents

say.text: Let's gather it up. Writing, gods, the afterlife, pyramids and law each have one clear example.

show.text: Writing: hieroglyphs for stone, hieratic for papyrus | Rosetta Stone: three scripts, read by 1822 | Gods: houses called temples | Afterlife: weighing of the heart | Pyramids: built by paid workers | Law: vizier, kenbet, ma'at

say.text: One last check. What links the weighing of the heart and the courts?

show.text: What links them?

ask.q: Which idea links the weighing of the heart and the law courts?
ask.why: The heart was weighed against Ma'at's feather. Courts were meant to uphold ma'at, and the vizier was called her priest.

say.text: Well done. Next class: Egypt III, with trade, everyday life and Egypt's neighbours.

show.text: Next: Egypt III: Trade, Everyday Life and Neighbours

frame_of_reference.when: About 2600 to 2500 BCE, when the Giza pyramids rose
frame_of_reference.elsewhere: In Peru, the city of Caral was being built at roughly the same time. NPR reports its buildings as about 4,600 years old, around the time of the Egyptian pyramids. Lesson 11 covers it.

frame_of_reference.when: Early Egyptian law, about 3000 BCE onward
frame_of_reference.elsewhere: Mesopotamia also had law, and Egyptian law ranks with Sumerian as one of the world's oldest surviving legal systems. Unlike Egypt, Mesopotamia left law codes such as Hammurabi's. Lesson 2 covers this.

frame_of_reference.when: 196 BCE, when the Rosetta Stone decree was written
frame_of_reference.elsewhere: Egypt was ruled by Greek-speaking Ptolemaic kings, which is why the decree includes Greek for the ruling elite.

frame_of_reference.when: 1799 to 1822, when the Rosetta Stone was found and read
frame_of_reference.elsewhere: France and Britain were great rivals. The stone passed to the British after the French defeat in 1801.

other_side.claim: The Giza pyramids were built by paid, well-fed Egyptian workers, not slaves.
other_side.other_view: The 'slave' idea comes from the Greek writer Herodotus, who wrote about 2,000 years later of gangs of 100,000 forced workers, which later retellings turned into slaves. Modern archaeology has not confirmed that picture. Estimates of the workforce also vary: 20,000 to 30,000 workers by one Egyptologists' count, and 'a few thousand' skilled craftsmen plus manual labourers by another description. Experts agree the builders were Egyptians but not on the exact numbers.

Thomas Young made early steps, including the name Ptolemy and the cartouche, and Champollion built on Young's method. It is unclear how much Champollion drew on Young's work. Champollion took the decipherment further and is the one widely credited.

other_side.claim: The Rosetta Stone belongs in the British Museum, where it has been since 1802.
other_side.other_view: Egypt has renewed calls for its return, including from archaeologist Zahi Hawass. The stone passed to Britain as a spoil of war, and Britain and France paid little attention to 'international norms' then. The sources I read do not give the museum's own reasons for keeping it.

other_side.claim: Egypt had no law code, and the legal system worked from decrees and precedent.
other_side.other_view: Some writers argue a code must have existed, because precedent was in use by the Early Dynastic Period. Others note that none has been found and that Egyptian law operated through decrees and earlier cases.

other_side.claim: The Diary of Merer shows how the Great Pyramid was built.
other_side.other_view: The diary is widely used as evidence for how stone reached Giza under Khufu. At least one scholar argues it needs careful re-examination, because the text has interpretive limits for claims about monumental construction.
